hello.note: Standard IRCAM greeting, used nationwide regardless of local variety (Tashelhit, Central Atlas, Tarifit); this file uses IRCAM Standard Moroccan Amazigh forms throughout.

good_morning.note: Literally 'lights/dawn'; azul also works generically for morning.

good_evening.note: Related to 'imensi' (evening meal); confirmed pre-rendered in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data, where it also serves as an evening parting phrase.

goodbye.note: Literally 'until we meet'; this is the form confirmed in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data. Ar tufat ('until tomorrow') is a Kabyle-attested alternative (Omniglot) also heard in Morocco.

how_are_you.note: To a woman: mamek tgit. Confirmed (minor schwa-spelling variation) in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data as 'Manmk tgid'/'Mamk tggid'.

thank_you.note: Confirmed exactly, pre-rendered in Tifinagh, in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data and the Omniglot Kabyle phrasebook.

youre_welcome.note: Rivals considered: ulac aghilif ('no worry', shared with no_problem, less dedicated) and s tumert ('with pleasure', thin evidence). Ansuf is the repeated Tatoeba translation of 'You're welcome' itself (Anṣuf yes-k/yes-m in Kabyle), and 'welcome' is independently attested in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) and Tashelhit (shi) Tatoeba data plus the Omniglot Kabyle phrasebook.

no_problem.note: Literally 'there's no problem'. Rivals considered: ulac aghilif (very common in Kabyle Tatoeba data, but 'aghilif' does not occur anywhere in the Standard Moroccan Tamazight/zgh corpus) and ula max (a thin, single-instance zgh dialogue reply). Ur illi umukris is the shipped pick as the consistently zgh-attested form, cross-confirmed by the Tashelhit phrase 'kra umukris' (a problem); ulac aghilif is kept as a well-known pan-Berber alternative.

please.note: Literally 'if you wish/want'; directly attested pre-rendered in Tifinagh in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data. Ttxil-k (to a man) / ttxil-m (to a woman), an Arabic-influenced borrowing, is the more common pan-Berber alternative (Kabyle, Tashelhit, general Berber data) but does not appear in the zgh-tagged data.

excuse_me.note: Used to get attention or ask someone to repeat themselves; literally 'pardon?/yes?' (from Arabic na'am). Directly attested in Kabyle Tatoeba data as 'Anɛam?' = 'Pardon me?/Excuse me?/Come again?'; not found in the smaller zgh/Tashelhit corpora, but likely a shared Arabic-derived interjection across varieties.

sorry.note: Literally 'forgive me'. Confirmed directly in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data ('assuref'/'ssuref iyi') and the Omniglot Kabyle phrasebook ('Suref-iyi').

yes.note: Confirmed directly and repeatedly in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data. Ih is a common alternative heard in Kabyle and several other varieties.

no.note: Confirmed directly and repeatedly in Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba data, where Ala also occurs as a common alternative; Kabyle instead favors Xati.

of_course.note: Literally 'it's obvious/clear'. Rivals considered from Kabyle Tatoeba data: Wamma! (a frequent single-word reply, but 'wamma' primarily means 'otherwise/or else' - its use here looks like a thin, loose one-off translation, so rejected); Ih, ih! (repeated 'yes, yes', plausible but generic); D ayen ibanen / Iban kan (fuller phrases on the same root). Iban stands alone as the direct, repeated translation of 'It's obvious.'/'That's obvious.' and is the semantic core shared by every candidate; zgh-specific evidence for this exact phrase is thin (one loose match using 'aad', lit. 'still/yet').

amazing.note: Confirmed by the cognate Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba form 'igrz' ('it's amazing'), same root.

delicious.note: Literally 'it's sweet'; root confirmed by the Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba form 'izid' ('it is delicious'). 'Immim' (yummy) is a common, more exclamatory alternative.

cheers.note: Literally 'may it give you(pl) health'; this is the Standard Moroccan Tamazight (zgh) Tatoeba form for 'Cheers!'. Kabyle instead favors 's tezmert-ik/-im' (to your strength, gendered singular) - a fine alternative when toasting one person. Toasting is not a deeply traditional custom in Morocco, so usage of any of these forms is thinner than most entries in this file.
